A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the revised numbering and placement.

before.justification: v1 reports original toy-model training experiments, parameter sweeps, and attention-decomposition analyses of GPT-2 and Pythia on indirect object identification.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original SAE-dictionary anisotropy measurements, controlled anisotropy experiments, and RoPE toy-model results.

M1.justification: The original autoencoder-attention model and sparse attention decomposition remain. v2 adds an experimental RoPE variant with position-dependent attention and target logits, and evaluates covariance anti-whitening of singular vectors.

E1.justification: Coverage expands within the existing toy-model and GPT-2 settings: v2 analyzes SAE dictionaries across GPT-2 Small's 12 layers and adds controlled anisotropic and position-dependent synthetic scenarios. The GPT-2/Pythia indirect object identification coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Figure 4 introduces an evaluated comparison between raw singular-vector alignment and covariance anti-whitened alignment. The existing spectrum-preserving random-rotation comparison in the language-model experiments remains unchanged.

E3.justification: The added studies introduce substantially different experimental designs. Appendix C.3 freezes dictionaries, sweeps anisotropy from 0 to 50, and trains only attention weights for 20,000 steps using a constant learning rate and no reconstruction loss; Appendix D introduces RoPE with context length 16, base 100, and mixed positional targets. These supplement the retained protocols.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends robustness analysis by measuring realistic anisotropy, testing alignment under controlled anisotropic distortion, and examining anti-whitening. The new RoPE study tests alignment with positional features and analyzes their allocation to frequency bands. Existing parameter sweeps and head-capacity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix C.3 reports five sampled anisotropy directions and mean plus or minus one standard deviation for Figure 4. The original five-seed summaries and 95% confidence intervals remain; no increase in the original experiments' run counts is established.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include layerwise SAE anisotropy measurements, alignment under distortion, and RoPE alignment and frequency-allocation findings. Figure 4 shows approximately 0.8 raw versus 0.9 anti-whitened alignment at anisotropy 50. These are newly reported results under new conditions, while the original experimental results are retained.

T1.justification: The original Appendix B assumptions and proofs are substantively retained; the exact-alignment theorem becomes Corollary 1 and subsequent theorems are renumbered. New mathematics includes the controlled covariance construction in Appendix C.3 and position-dependent attention, frequency-band decomposition, and target definitions in Appendix D, Equations 17–19.

C1.justification: The four main contributions remain: alignment in toy models, alignment of leading singular vectors with important features, feature orthogonalization, and sparse attention decomposition in real models. The rewritten conclusion preserves their scope and the proposed interpretability application.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the added evidence as showing that strong anisotropy need not destroy alignment and that anti-whitening can help. It also explains RoPE frequency allocation through positional sensitivity and clarifies the spectral-concentration alternative to alignment. The limitations concerning direct real-model feature identification and multi-head behavior remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, SAE source and normalization details, and implementation settings for the new studies. Section 5 newly specifies 128 GPT-2 IOI prompts varying names, templates, and objects; this is additional documentation, not evidence of an increased sample size.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly credits prior empirical demonstrations of alignment instead of primarily describing an assumed relationship. It replaces the activation-patching critique with probing and causal-intervention literature and adds references supporting the SAE, anisotropy, and RoPE analyses. The central positioning around explaining why and when alignment occurs remains.

P1.justification: Localized revisions expand the theoretical explanation and training-dynamics discussion, revise the background paragraph, and create a separate Conclusions section. New appendix subsections accompany the added studies, but most existing prose and the overall narrative sequence are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds a complete toy-model schematic and plots for anisotropy, RoPE alignment, and frequency-band allocation. Existing figures and both tables are largely preserved, with resizing, relocation, caption refinements, and renumbering rather than a wholesale visual redesign.

improvement.justification: The new anisotropy and RoPE studies directly investigate applicability concerns that v1 left largely unexplored, while the model schematic, code link, and additional experimental details improve clarity and reproducibility. The gains remain limited: the added studies are preliminary, the foundational proofs are unchanged, and direct validation of feature identities in real models remains outside scope.
